title: NLRB v. Bell Aerospace Co. (1974)
summary: The National Labor Relations Act excludes all true managerial employees from its protections, and the Board may decide who is managerial through case-by-case adjudication rather than rulemaking.
notes:
Key line: The views expressed in Chenery II and Wyman-Gordon make plain that the Board is not precluded from announcing new principles in an adjudicative proceeding and that the choice between rulemaking and adjudication lies in the first instance within the Board's discretion. (Justice Powell)

Citation: 416 U.S. 267 (1974).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was the National Labor Relations Board. The respondent was Bell Aerospace Company, a division of Textron, Inc., which operated a plant in Wheatfield, New York, engaged in research and development in the design and fabrication of aerospace products. The union seeking to represent the company's buyers was Amalgamated Local No. 1286 of the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America, which filed an amicus brief urging reversal of the decision below. The Chamber of Commerce of the United States filed an amicus brief on the other side. Norton J. Come argued for the Board and Richard E. Moot for the company.
sections.Material Facts: On July 30, 1970, the union petitioned the Board for a representation election among the twenty-five buyers in the purchasing and procurement department at the Wheatfield plant. The buyers purchased materials and components, selected vendors, negotiated prices and committed the company's funds, subject to review above set dollar limits. The company argued that buyers were managerial employees excluded from the Act. The Board's Regional Director found the buyers an appropriate unit, and the Board affirmed, stating that even if buyers were managerial employees they were covered by the Act unless their union activity would create a conflict of interest in labor relations. That position departed from earlier Board decisions holding that all managerial employees were excluded. The buyers voted for the union, the Board certified it, and the company refused to bargain. The Board found the refusal an unfair labor practice under sections 8(a)(5) and (1) and ordered bargaining.
sections.Procedural History: The Board petitioned the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit for enforcement of its bargaining order. The court denied enforcement, 475 F.2d 485 (1973), on two grounds: it was unclear whether the Board had found the buyers not to be true managerial employees or had adopted a new and erroneous view that managerial employees are covered absent a conflict of interest, and in any event the Board, having reversed its long-standing position, was required to proceed by rulemaking rather than adjudication. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, heard argument on January 14, 1974, and decided the case on April 23, 1974. It affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded. Justice Powell wrote for the Court.
sections.Issue: Two questions were presented. First, did Congress intend to exclude from the protections of the National Labor Relations Act all employees properly classified as managerial, or only those managerial employees whose unionization would create a conflict of interest in labor relations? Second, if the Board on remand were to determine that the company's buyers are not managerial employees, contrary to its own prior decisions, must it make that determination through the rulemaking procedures of the Administrative Procedure Act rather than through adjudication in an unfair labor practice proceeding?
sections.Holding: Congress intended to exclude from the Act all employees properly classified as managerial, not merely those in positions susceptible to conflicts of interest; the Board's early decisions, the purpose and legislative history of the Taft-Hartley amendments of 1947, more than two decades of Board construction and the decisions of the courts of appeals all confirm this reading. The Board is not required to proceed by rulemaking to decide whether buyers or some buyers are managerial. Under SEC v. Chenery and NLRB v. Wyman-Gordon the Board may announce new principles in adjudication, and the choice between rulemaking and adjudication lies in the first instance in the Board's discretion. Given the variety of buyers' duties across industries, case-by-case development is reasonable. The Court expressed no view on whether these buyers are managerial and remanded.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Powell first reviewed the meaning of managerial employee. From 1946 the Board had excluded executives who formulate and effectuate management policies, and when Congress in 1947 excluded supervisors it acted on the understanding that managerial employees were already outside the Act. For over twenty years after Taft-Hartley the Board continued to exclude all managerial employees, and the courts of appeals uniformly agreed. The Board's new conflict-of-interest test in 1970 therefore departed from the statute as Congress and the Board had long understood it. On the second question Powell turned to Chenery II, where the Court held that an agency may apply a general standard first announced in an adjudication because problems may arise that the agency could not reasonably foresee or that require case-by-case treatment, and to Wyman-Gordon, where six Justices recognized that the Board's choice between rulemaking and adjudication lies primarily within its informed discretion. Those cases make plain that the Board is not precluded from announcing new principles in adjudication. There might be situations where reliance on adjudication would be an abuse of discretion, but nothing here justified that conclusion: the company knew the issue and had a full chance to litigate it, and no fines or damages were at stake. Because buyers' duties vary widely across companies and industries, a general rule would have marginal utility, and the Board reasonably proceeds by attention to the specific authority of buyers in each company.

topics.lrs-o-retroactivity: Adjudication remained available while serious reliance concerns were reserved; no damages, fines, or penalties were being imposed in the setting described.
topics.lrs-o-apa-classification: The Board's freedom to choose adjudication over rulemaking rests on the APA's distinction between orders and rules.
topics.lrs-k-legislative-history: The Court's exclusion of managerial employees rested on the Taft-Hartley Act's legislative history.

learning.separateOpinions: Five to four on the first question, unanimous on the second. Justice White, joined by Justices Brennan, Stewart and Marshall, dissented in part. He agreed that the Board need not resort to rulemaking, but he would have deferred to the Board's reading that the Act excludes only those managerial employees whose unionization would create a conflict of interest, finding the statutory text and history less clear than the majority did.
